builtFrom.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of solids and liquids; How heating and cooling change state; Scientific thinking helps solve everyday problems

s.d: Students draw examples of solids and liquids on a Freeform board and drag them into groups after observing classroom samples. Sorting by properties helps them explain what they can actually see rather than guessing from a material's name. Another pair challenges one choice, such as sand that pours but has solid grains, and students move or revise their drawings. The finished board has grouped drawings and short notes explaining the tricky choices.

Students enter the number of ice cubes still containing solid ice at regular intervals into a teacher-prepared Excel table. The changing numbers help them track melting rather than relying on a final look. Groups choose two classroom locations and keep the starting ice cubes, containers and checking times the same. Students turn their table into a column chart showing where solid ice remained longer.
s.quote: Using tables, drawings or diagrams to represent melting or freezing.
s.link: A table and chart make the planned melting observations easier to compare across time.

s.d: Students draw the stages of ceramic making in Book Creator and add short captions explaining what water, air or heat changes. This helps them distinguish clay drying from the lasting changes caused by firing. They ask another pair to read the pages and flag any caption that suggests fired clay can turn back into workable clay with water. Their finished book gives the art room a student-written guide from wet clay to finished pottery.

Students draw their first prediction about melting chocolate beside what they observed, then record a short explanation in Explain Everything. Comparing the two helps them explain how observations changed their thinking about heating materials. A partner asks which observation supports the explanation before the student records a final version. The result is a short recording with drawings and spoken reasons, rather than a retelling of every experiment step.
s.quote: Considering how their thinking has changed through observations and experiments.
s.link: A before-and-after explanation makes the planned reflection specific to evidence from the melting investigation.

s.d: Students write and lay out a Canva instruction sheet for repeating their freezing-water investigation, using numbered text boxes and drawn shapes. Clear steps show how careful scientific thinking helps someone else investigate a material change. Another group follows the instructions with teacher supervision and marks any missing details on paper so the writers can revise their design. The class keeps the corrected instruction sheets as a set of repeatable investigations.
s.quote: Demonstrating understanding through posters, procedural texts, or oral presentations.
s.link: Testing the procedural text with another group gives students a real reason to make their scientific instructions precise.

stem.d: Students design and build a small ice-saving shelter from recycled cardboard, fabric scraps and foil, with a removable cup holding an ice cube. They sketch a plan and choose how to slow melting, using their observations of heating and cooling. Groups test their shelters beside an uncovered cup with equal-sized ice cubes in the same location, then change one part and test again. Using the built-in iPad Camera, they photograph each design and its ice at agreed times without moving the cups. At the end, students demonstrate the opening shelter and use their photographs to explain which change helped ice stay solid longer.
stem.quote: Using knowledge of changes of state to explain real-life examples (e.g. melting chocolate, freezing water).
stem.link: Building and improving an ice shelter applies observations of melting to the everyday problem of keeping something frozen.

builtFrom.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
builtFrom.lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Students draw the same familiar playground scene twice in Brushes Redux, changing colours and brush marks to show two different feelings. This helps them explore how digital art can express different understandings of the same place. A partner looks at both drawings and guesses which choices made the playground feel welcoming or unsettling. Students keep two contrasting digital paintings and explain one change that affected the meaning.
s.quote: They will learn foundational skills such as taking well-composed photographs with an iPad and using the basic drawing and editing tools in apps like Brushes Redux and PicEdu.
s.link: This builds on exploring drawing and editing tools by giving students a clear reason to change their artistic choices.

s.d: Students record short musical parts in GarageBand to represent features of the picture book image used in music. Choosing sounds and combining parts helps them express how they understand the image without adding words. Each group chooses two instruments, then tests whether changing an instrument changes what classmates imagine. They keep a short instrumental composition with separate tracks for their musical parts.
s.activity: Composition inspired by a picture book
s.quote: Music: students worked in small groups to create a composition inspired by a picture book image.
s.link: This extends the group composition activity by letting students record separate parts and listen to how different instruments affect the image's meaning.

s.d: Students photograph a paper face frame by frame in Stop Motion Studio, moving loose paper eyebrows and a mouth to change its expression. This makes them look closely at how small visual changes communicate feelings. Another group watches without being told the intended feeling and points out the frame where the expression becomes clear. Students finish with a silent animation showing one expression gradually changing into another.
s.quote: They look into the universal facial expressions and further build their understanding on reading expressions and changing expressions to communicate feelings in various situations…
s.link: This builds on reading and changing facial expressions by slowing the changes down so students can examine each movement.

s.d: Students draw two outfits in Book Creator and add short French opinions using the colour and clothing words practised in class. Their pages explore how words and images work together to express personal taste. Students deliberately give the same outfit different opinions on two pages, then ask a classmate whether both opinions make sense. They make a short illustrated French book with drawings and editable text.
s.quote: Focus on vocabulary for colours, clothes, and giving opinions "That is a sporty/relaxed/chic outfit."
s.link: This builds on French clothing vocabulary and opinions by pairing students' own outfit drawings with contrasting written responses.

s.d: Students draw figures in Freeform to show two body positions they explored during the dramatic tension movement activity. Arranging these drawings helps them explain how a body can express different levels of tension. Partners duplicate a drawing and change just the shoulders or hands, then compare which version communicates more tension. Each pair makes a board of contrasting poses with short explanations beside them.
s.quote: Dramatic Tension Term 2 - students explore 'tension' as a physical movement activity, understanding how we hold tension and express different levels of tension depending on our circumstance.
s.link: This builds on the movement activity by letting students redraw and compare the body positions that communicate tension.

stem.d: Students design and build a cardboard face with sliding paper eyebrows and a mouth moved by card strips through slots. They first sketch how the moving parts could communicate two different feelings, connecting their build to the facial expression activities. Using cereal boxes, split pins and tape, they make a prototype and ask a partner to identify each expression without a spoken clue. They adjust the slots or moving pieces when a feeling is unclear, then test again. Students demonstrate a working face that changes expression and point out the alteration that made its message clearer.
stem.quote: They look into the universal facial expressions and further build their understanding on reading expressions and changing expressions to communicate feelings in various situations…
stem.link: This extends changing facial expressions into a physical design challenge where students test whether moving features communicate their intended feeling.

builtFrom.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

s.d: Students write a short Padlet post naming an invention and the need or want they think led to it. This gives the class a starting point for discussing why people invent things. The teacher displays the posts, and students choose one idea they disagree with and explain their thinking aloud. The class ends with a board of starting ideas to revisit after exploring digital systems.
s.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
s.link: This builds on the prior knowledge task by collecting ideas about the problems inventions solve.

s.d: Students build a Freeform mind map with boxes for a computer's hardware, software and connections. This helps them work out which parts do different jobs when a device sends a picture. Partners follow the arrows on each other's boards and point out any missing steps or unclear connections. Each pair finishes with a revised diagram showing how they think a picture travels between devices.
s.quote: What happens inside our computers and networks when we send a message or a picture to someone else?
s.link: This develops the planned computer mind map by showing how parts work together when sending a picture.

s.d: Students collect class votes on which everyday classroom problem most needs an invention, then enter the totals in Excel. Comparing needs and wants helps them choose a problem worth solving. Each pair makes a column chart and a bar chart from the same totals, then chooses which is easier for another pair to read. They finish with a spreadsheet containing the votes, both charts and a sentence explaining their choice.
s.quote: AC9M3ST02 create and compare different graphical representations of data sets including using software where appropriate; interpret the data in terms of the context…
s.link: This gives the planned data collection and graph comparison a practical purpose: choosing a classroom problem to solve.

s.d: Students draw a school plan on a floor mat and program Sphero BOLT to carry a pretend message between two buildings. This shows how programmed instructions can meet a need to move something from one place to another. Another pair chooses a path closure, so students must change their turns and travel times rather than move the buildings. They finish with a tested route that reaches its destination without crossing the closed path.
s.quote: Elaborations: creating a two-dimensional plan of the school on a floor mat, representing key buildings and landmarks, then programming a robot to move to different locations within the space.
s.link: This follows the planned school map and robot task, adding a reason to test and change the instructions.

s.d: Students draw a fictional online situation in Seesaw and add two possible responses as text. This puts safe and responsible choices alongside the reasons people want to communicate online. A partner reads the situation, chooses the safer response and explains their choice aloud before the author revises any confusing wording. The finished Seesaw page has a situation, two choices and an explanation of the safer action, without anyone's personal details.
s.quote: Antony sparked discussion about balancing screen time with real-world play and how unplugging from devices can spark creativity and connection, while The Internet is a Puddle by Shona Innes helped students identify safe versus risky online situations - a lesson reinforced through the Safe vs Risky Puddles Seesaw activity.
s.link: This builds on the planned Seesaw safety activity by asking students to write situations that others can work through.

stem.d: Students ask another group what makes passing classroom messages difficult, then sketch and build a hand-powered delivery system using cardboard towers, string, paper cups and tape. This explores how a real need can lead to an invention without needing a screen. Groups test whether their carrier can move a folded message across a table gap without dropping it, then change the cup attachment or string supports and test again. Another group tries the revised machine and suggests one improvement. Students demonstrate a successful delivery and point to the part they changed after testing.
stem.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
stem.link: This turns the planned question about designing solutions into a physical invention that students test and improve.

builtFrom.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals; Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly; First Nations knowledge of soils and rocks

s.d: Students build a branching identification guide that asks about visible soil components and leads to a likely sample match. This makes them choose which soil properties actually distinguish their samples, using a blank branching form the teacher prepares. A buddy class tests the guide against numbered samples and reports incorrect matches through the form. Students revise the questions, and the teacher assesses whether their guide reliably separates the samples.
s.transforms: learning, goals: Students build and revise an identification tool through sample testing; assessment judges its reliability.
s.quote: Finding out: Science Investigation: Students classify and compare soil/rock samples, describing their observable properties.
s.link: The sample comparison becomes a working identification guide that another class checks against the actual soils.

s.d: Students create a linked book that lets younger students choose an everyday use, then follow links to suitable rocks or minerals. This connects observable properties with uses such as pencils and buildings, starting from a linked page template the teacher prepares. Year 1 students use the book to answer material-choice questions and identify confusing routes. The teacher assesses the accuracy of the choices and explanations, and students repair links or explanations that misled readers.
s.transforms: learning, goals: Younger students test material choices using the linked guide; assessment examines its accuracy and explanations.

s.d: Students enter counts of pebbles and plant fragments from equal-sized soil samples into a shared table and create comparison charts. This shows how soils differ, using a labelled spreadsheet the teacher prepares. A buddy teacher uses the charts to choose two contrasting samples for a class investigation, then checks that choice against the actual samples. The teacher assesses whether the class's data supported a sound choice, and students correct unclear labels or counting errors.
s.transforms: learning, goals: Another teacher uses the data to select samples and checks the decision; assessment judges the data's usefulness.
s.quote: Finding out: Science Investigation: Students classify and compare soil/rock samples, describing their observable properties.
s.link: The local soil observations become a comparison table another class uses to select contrasting investigation samples.

s.d: Students design a comparison poster showing how one rock or mineral's properties suit two everyday uses. They connect those uses with a practical suggestion for using that resource responsibly. Partners read the poster at its intended display size and identify any claim that lacks an explanation or readable label. Students revise the layout and wording before printing a poster that connects properties, uses and a responsible choice.
s.transforms: Digital layout and peer feedback improve the planned poster without changing its purpose or assessment.

s.d: Students read community-endorsed First Nations resources selected and linked by the teacher about ochre or grindstones. They add a short explanation of one use, its cultural value and the source it came from. Partners comment with a question that the original writer checks against the same source rather than guessing an answer. The class ends with a searchable board of sourced explanations and clearly marked unanswered questions.
s.transforms: Searchable explanations and source-checked discussion improve sharing and research within the existing cultural knowledge task.
s.quote: Cultural Knowledge: Students explain how First Nations Australians use a particular rock, mineral, or soil resource and reflect on its value.
s.link: The cultural knowledge explanation includes clear sources and questions that keep First Nations accounts at the centre.

stem.d: Students design small sieves from cardboard frames and different mesh scraps to separate pebbles from equal amounts of dry, safe soil. The teacher provides a Micro:bit starter program that uses its accelerometer to count shakes while the device is secured to the frame. Teams compare separation after the same shake count, then change the mesh or frame after checking what passed through. They demonstrate a revised sieve and explain which soil components it separates reliably.
stem.transforms: Accelerometer counts make repeated sieve tests more consistent and give students evidence for changing their physical designs.
stem.quote: Finding out: Science Investigation: Students classify and compare soil/rock samples, describing their observable properties.
stem.link: Building and testing sieves gives students another way to compare the components found in their local soil samples.

units.th: Where We Are in Place and Time

builtFrom.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
builtFrom.lo: How Australia and neighbouring regions define places; Australia's states/territories have unique identities; First Nations connections to Country

s.d: Students sketch a favourite school place in Freeform, then add notes showing what makes it meaningful to them. This shows how the same place can matter to people for different reasons. Partners compare drawings of the same location and add a question beside something they see differently. Each student finishes with a board containing their sketch, their reasons and a partner's question.

Students examine the displayed objects and photographs from Australia's neighbours, then type an observation and a question on a teacher-prepared Padlet board. Their different responses show that people can read the same representation of a place differently. Each pair chooses another pair's question and adds a comment suggesting what they could look at more closely. The class has a question board to revisit as they learn about neighbouring places.
s.quote: Tuning in/Provocations Tuning in 1 - get a collection of artefacts, photos, dot paintings, stuff from TI Learning Asian/Pacific neighbours.
s.link: This keeps the planned close observation and gives students a shared place to collect and revisit their questions.

s.d: Students explore Australia and nearby Asian countries in Google Maps, zooming out to check directions and zooming in to inspect coastlines. Changing the scale shows how a map can represent the same place in different ways. Partners take turns giving a direction clue while the other finds the country, without using a student login. Each pair ends by pointing out a neighbour and explaining its position relative to Australia.
s.quote: Learn about where they are situated in relation to Australia.
s.link: This gives students a map they can move and zoom while practising the planned compass directions.

s.d: Students build a short Book Creator book about an Australian place, using typed explanations and their own drawings to show how people could respect it. They explain why the place matters, recognising that different people may value it differently. A partner checks whether each suggested action would genuinely help that particular place, and the author revises one page. The finished book pairs practical advice with a reason for each action.
s.activity: Showing respect for an Australian place
s.quote: Choose a place or feature of Australia and write and how and why people could show respect for it.
s.link: This turns the planned writing about respect into an illustrated book with advice students can check and improve.

s.d: Students open a teacher-uploaded copy of their original world map in Seesaw and draw additions in a different colour. They add a typed note explaining what their map now shows and something it still leaves out. Students choose one change they think would most help a younger child understand Australia or its neighbours. Their completed comparison keeps the original thinking visible beside the new map details and explanation.
s.activity: Adding new learning to original maps

stem.d: Students plan and build a cardboard relief map of a small Australian coastal area, using folded paper for hills, wool for rivers and removable clear packaging for a state boundary overlay. The separate layers show that physical features and government boundaries represent place differently. Pairs ask another group to trace a river and locate the boundary, then adjust any confusing shapes or lines. They use Micro:bit buttons to display either an arrow pointing north or a heart marking a place they value, with its position chosen on the model. Each group demonstrates how lifting the boundary layer changes what the map shows without changing the land underneath.
stem.quote: what are some of the natural and man Museum Vic resources can made borders/boundaries in Australia and support this inquiry the region?
stem.link: This builds on the planned boundary discussion by letting students construct, test and revise a map with removable layers.

builtFrom.ci: The choices and actions we make contribute to our health and wellbeing.
builtFrom.lo: What it means to be healthy; Choices and their impact on health; Actions to maintain a healthy mind and body

s.d: Students draw friendly classroom actions and arrange them on a shared Freeform board in small groups. They explain how including someone or listening carefully can help people feel safe and well. Another group moves similar drawings together and adds a sticky note suggesting an action that is missing. The finished board is a class collection of practical choices that support everyone's wellbeing.
s.quote: Finding Out Develop a list of things students can do to We are a friendly class because...
s.link: This builds on the friendly class list by letting students group their drawings and suggest missing actions.

s.d: Students write and illustrate two possible endings to one of the planned Friendship Fire scenarios in Book Creator. Each ending shows how a different choice could affect someone's feelings and wellbeing. Partners read both endings and suggest where a character could pause, ask for help or make amends. Students finish with a short illustrated book that compares the consequences of two choices.
s.quote: Can you sort out these Friendship Fires? Read all six scenarios and then select two to write about.
s.link: This extends the scenario writing by showing how two different responses can change what happens next.

s.d: Students draw a fictional everyday situation for each mood meter colour and record a short explanation in Seesaw. They suggest a safe action that might help the character look after their mind or body. Partners listen and offer another possible strategy, without asking anyone to describe private experiences. Each student keeps an illustrated recording of feelings and practical ways to respond.
s.quote: Reflect on one feeling from each colour group and explain your emotional experiences.
s.link: This keeps the mood meter reflection while giving students a safe way to explain feelings through fictional situations.

s.d: Students design a two-page Canva goal card showing one healthy teamwork choice they want to practise. They explain how listening, taking turns or asking calmly for help could support their own wellbeing and someone else's. After a planned group task, a partner gives one specific suggestion and students revise their card. Their finished card shows the original goal, useful feedback and a next step they can actually try.
s.quote: Why is it important to listen to feedback and use it to grow…
s.link: This gives the planned feedback and goal setting a practical focus on choices that support healthy relationships.

s.d: Students build a short GarageBand piece in pairs, taking turns to choose and arrange loops. They notice how sharing decisions and responding respectfully can help both partners feel included and ready to keep trying. Halfway through, each pair plays its piece to another pair and asks for one manageable suggestion. They revise the music and keep the finished piece as something they made through cooperation and persistence.
s.quote: Music - In music, students practised working in small groups to create music together.
s.link: This builds on the planned group music task with a clear chance to practise feedback, persistence and fair decision making.

stem.d: Students sketch and build a handheld cardboard slider with paper windows, split pins and popstick tabs that reveal possible responses to a Friendship Fire. They choose prompts such as pausing, listening or getting help, explaining how each could protect someone's wellbeing. Another pair tests the prototype against two planned scenarios, checking whether the tabs move easily and the advice makes sense, before the makers improve it. Students demonstrate their revised slider by moving through a scenario and explaining why a different situation might need a different response.
stem.quote: Can you sort out these Friendship Fires? Read all six scenarios and then select two to write about.
stem.link: This turns the planned scenario discussion into a working object students can test and improve with different friendship problems.
